summary: Describes the queries a DNS resolver should send to initialize its cache, so it gets a current NS record set for the root zone and address information for the root servers. It is a Best Current Practice and obsoletes RFC 8109.

eli5.summary: A new resolver begins knowing nothing. This tells it which first questions to ask to learn where the top-level helpers are.

questions: how does a resolver find the root servers
subtitle: The first question a DNS resolver asks to learn where the root servers are, and how to ask it safely.

tldr.problem: A recursive resolver starts with an empty cache and only a configured list of root server addresses, which can go stale when root server addresses change.
tldr.mechanism: The resolver sends a priming query (QNAME '.', QTYPE NS, QCLASS IN, RD bit 0) to a randomly chosen configured address and caches the NS RRset and the address records in the response.
tldr.outcome: The resolver ends up with a current list of root server names and addresses. The RFC warns that priming responses cannot be protected by DNSSEC today, so spoofing remains a risk.

today: RFC 9609 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 209) and obsoletes RFC 8109. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Resolvers Need Priming
sections.content:
Recursive DNS resolvers need a starting point. RFC 1034 describes a common scenario: the resolver begins with an empty cache and some configuration for finding the names and addresses of the DNS root servers. This document covers that common implementation choice, and only for recursive resolvers and the IN class.

The RFC points out that it is not the only way to start with an empty cache. Some implementers took other directions, some of which fail, sometimes disastrously. For example, an implementation that only takes root server addresses from configuration, and not from the DNS as described here, will have stale data that could cause slower resolution.
sections.eli5: A new resolver knows nothing, so it needs a first step to find out where to start asking.

sections.title: What Priming Is
sections.content:
Priming is the act of finding the list of root servers from a configuration that lists some or all of their purported IP addresses. The resolver starts with no cached information about the root servers and finishes with a full list of their names and addresses in its cache. RFC 1034 calls the configured list the 'SBELT', a safety belt structure.

The configured addresses usually come from the vendor or distributor of the software and may become outdated. The root server names are called the root server identifiers. The list of identifiers has been stable since 1997, but their IPv4 and IPv6 addresses occasionally change, and research cited in the RFC indicates some resolvers fail to update after such changes. That is why resolvers should cope with change without waiting for an operator to update configuration.

The priming information can be in any format that gives the software the addresses of at least some root server identifiers. The root hints file published by IANA is one example; its names are harmless but not useful for priming. A resolver that serves a local copy of the root zone, as in RFC 8806, primes in the same way.
sections.eli5: Your old list of phone numbers might have wrong numbers on it, so you ask for a fresh list instead of trusting the old one.

sections.title: The Priming Query
sections.content:
A priming query is a normal DNS query with a QNAME of ., a QTYPE of NS and a QCLASS of IN, sent to one of the configured addresses. It can use UDP or TCP. Over UDP the source port SHOULD be randomly selected (RFC 5452) to hamper on-path attacks, and DNS cookies (RFC 7873) can also help. The Recursion Desired (RD) bit SHOULD be set to 0.

The resolver SHOULD use EDNS0 (RFC 6891) and SHOULD announce and handle a reassembly size of at least 1024 octets, so a full priming response fits.

The resolver SHOULD send a priming query only when needed, for example with an empty cache or when the root NS RRset has expired by its TTL. It MAY pre-fetch the RRset before expiry, and then SHOULD use the addresses in its cache rather than its configuration. If a query gets no response, the resolver MUST retry with a different configured address. Targets SHOULD be chosen randomly to spread load, and it may prefer IPv4 or IPv6 depending on connectivity.
sections.eli5: You ask one helper, picked at random, 'who are all the main helpers?' and if they do not answer you try a different one.

sections.title: The Priming Response
sections.content:
A root server cannot tell a priming query from any other query for the root NS RRset, so its response is a normal DNS response. The response MUST have an RCODE of NOERROR and the AA bit set. It MUST have the NS RRset in the Answer section and an empty Authority section, plus an Additional section with A and AAAA RRsets for the servers named. The resolver SHOULD treat it like any other data for its cache and SHOULD NOT expect 13 NS records, because some root servers have historically returned fewer.

At publication there were 13 root server operators running more than 1500 instances, each with one IPv4 and one IPv6 address. All the address records together exceed the original 512-octet limit of RFC 1035, so the Additional section may omit some. Re-sending the query does not help against servers that return a fixed order, so the resolver needs to ask directly for the A and AAAA RRsets of the remaining names.

Servers are not required to set the TC bit when addresses are left out. RFC 9471 requires TC for missing glue in referrals, but a priming response is not a referral, so its addresses are not glue and there is no requirement on how many addresses it includes.
sections.eli5: The answer is a list of names with their addresses. If the list is too long to fit, some addresses are left off, so you ask for those separately.

sections.title: Security and DNSSEC Limits
sections.content:
The root NS RRset is signed and can be validated. But at publication the addresses of those servers live in the root-servers.net zone, which is not signed, so the A and AAAA RRsets cannot be validated. An attacker who spoofs a priming response can substitute addresses under the attacker's control and redirect all of the victim resolver's queries.

A rogue root server can see all queries and alter unsigned parts of responses such as referral NS sets and glue. A resolver that follows referrals without separately querying the authoritative NS and address records of a TLD can be fooled, and the RFC says such an attacker effectively controls the whole name space for non-validating resolvers and for unsigned delegations. A validating resolver can detect attacks only for zones that are signed.

If the naming of root servers later moves into a signed zone, validating priming queries might become valuable. The RFC also notes that this document has no IANA actions.

Until priming responses are protected with DNSSEC, the RFC says there is no definitive way to prevent this kind of redirection.
sections.eli5: If a trickster answers your phone call before the real helper, you might be handed a fake list. A seal on the list would fix that, but the list of addresses has no seal yet.

sections.title: After Priming and Changes from RFC 8109
sections.content:
After priming, the resolver chooses among the cached NS records for each query it cannot answer from cache. Two common strategies are using the fastest server always, or grouping servers into buckets of fastness and picking randomly in a bucket. The RFC states no preference, other than suggesting resolvers not treat the root zone as special.

The appendix lists changes from RFC 8109. They include a new section on the content of priming information, text on the TC bit and on RFC 9471, the term 'root server identifiers', a note on post-priming strategies, the note about RFC 8806, and raising the expectations in Section 4.1 to MUST-level.
sections.eli5: Once you have the list you can pick whichever helper you like, and this document does not say which is best.
